markets.trajectory_note: CRITICAL REGULATORY CHANGE. Resolution 561 bars regulated electronic-FX providers - payment institutions, e-money issuers and acquirers - from using stablecoins or other crypto to settle the offshore leg of cross-border payments. Effective October 2026, settlement with overseas counterparties must run through traditional FX operations or non-resident real accounts. Brazil's crypto framework took effect February 2026 under Central Bank supervision: Resolution 519 established VASP licensing, Resolution 520 set minimum capital of R$10.8m-R$37.2m by activity type. IMPLICATION: the regulated-FX-provider channel is closing in Brazil precisely as Yellow Card expands there. Do not score Brazil on friction alone - the binding constraint is now regulatory and it is tightening.
markets.regulatory_detail: No presence. Resolution 519 VASP licensing regime in force from Feb 2026; Resolution 561 restricts stablecoin settlement of the offshore leg from Oct 2026.
markets.expansion_signal: DOWNGRADED. Pix has already removed most domestic rail friction (79.8bn transactions in 2025, 54.7% of retail payments) and Resolution 561 closes the regulated-FX-provider route. Large market, narrowing opening.

latam_context.adoption: 71% of Latin American firms already use stablecoins for cross-border payments (Fireblocks, 2025). B2B stablecoin payments rose from under $100m per month in early 2023 to over $6bn per month by mid-2025.
latam_context.baseline_friction: Correspondent banking settlement takes 3-5 business days; all-in costs reach 2-7% once wire fees, FX markups and intermediary deductions are counted. Sub-Saharan African remittance corridors still average over 6% in fees (World Bank).
latam_context.why_it_matters: Adoption is already high in LatAm, so the pitch there is displacement rather than education - a different sale from Africa. Worth stating in the market view.

blocked_funds_context.nigeria_historical_peak: Nigeria held the largest blocked-funds position in the world for over a year - USD549m in December 2022, USD662m in January 2023, USD743.7m by March 2023 per IATA correspondence to the aviation ministry. Fully resolved and off the list by 2026. Evidence that these positions do clear, and the reason Nigerian aviation treasury behaviour remains cautious.
blocked_funds_context.afraa_framing: AFRAA policy paper, July 2026: cash flow is the most pressing factor affecting the commercial viability of most African airlines; repatriation delays contravene bilateral air service agreements and occasion significant opportunity costs and foreign exchange losses. AFRAA's own recommendations include facilitating payments through international payment platforms - an explicit opening for settlement infrastructure.
blocked_funds_context.iata_framing: Willie Walsh, IATA Director General: timely repatriation is vital for airlines to cover dollar-denominated expenses, delays and denials increase exchange rate risks, and airlines operate on very thin margins. This is the clearest third-party articulation of the soft-currency-in, hard-currency-out problem available.
